summary.text: Scatter-brained Titan son of Iapetus, 'from the first a mischief to men who eat bread': forgetting his brother Prometheus' warning never to accept a gift from Olympian Zeus, he took in the moulded maiden — and with her the jar whose opening ended mankind's life without ills.
Son of Iapetus and brother of Prometheus and Atlas, who was given Pandora, the woman fashioned of clay, in marriage; their daughter is Pyrrha, wife of Deucalion and mother of the renewed human race.

story.text: An Oceanid bore him to the Titan Iapetus, last of four brothers in whom the fates of gods and men were knotted: stout-hearted Atlas, outrageous Menoetius, Prometheus subtle and shifting in counsel, and scatter-brained Epimetheus. Where his brother's name means Forethought, his means Afterthought — and Hesiod hangs the whole story of mankind's ruin on that difference. His mother is Clymene in Hesiod and in Hyginus' genealogy, Asia in Apollodorus.

Prometheus had warned him plainly: never take a gift of Olympian Zeus, but send it back, for fear it prove some harm to men. Then the Father sent the glorious Argus-Slayer, swift messenger of the gods, leading the maiden the gods had fashioned as a gift to Epimetheus — and Epimetheus did not think on what Prometheus had said. He took the gift; and afterwards, when the evil thing was already his, he understood.

Before that day, Hesiod says, the tribes of men lived on earth remote and free from ills, hard toil and heavy sickness. But once she was under Epimetheus' roof, the woman took the great lid off the jar with her hands and scattered all that was inside it, and her thought caused sorrow and mischief to men. Only Hope remained within, under the rim of the great jar — and countless plagues now wander silent among mankind, for Zeus took away their voice.

The later mythographers make the union a plain marriage and give it issue. In Hyginus, Pandora is given in wedlock to Epimetheus, Prometheus' brother, and from her is born Pyrrha; Apollodorus calls Pyrrha the daughter of Epimetheus and of Pandora, the first woman fashioned by the gods. Ovid, telling the flood, needs only a patronymic — Pyrrha is 'Epimethis', the daughter of Epimetheus — so that through her, and her stone-born children with Deucalion, the heedless Titan stands grandfather to the renewed human race and to Hellen, name-giver of the Hellenes.
